description: We're a team from Toronto who believe NASA's view of our planet should belong to everyone, not just people who can see a screen. We built Earth Jukebox over one weekend, rewriting it again and again until it felt right: we tuned every sound against real NASA frames, rebuilt the design from scratch when it didn't feel honest, and tested the page with a screen reader ourselves to hear what a blind visitor would hear. We care about one thing: that anyone, anywhere, can hear the planet change.
summary: Earth Jukebox turns NASA Earth Information Center visualizations into live, calm music, so anyone, including blind and low-vision people, can hear the planet change. A scan line moves across each NASA video frame and the site reads its real colours: warm ocean water plays high notes, cold plays low, city lights and lightning ring as chimes, and the yearly rise and fall of carbon dioxide sounds like a breath. Before the music, every track explains what each sound means. Listeners can also explore by touch or keyboard and hear each place described in words. It matters because NASA's Earth science is shared mostly as pictures, which leaves out people who can't see them.
details:
What it does: Earth Jukebox is a web page with four tracks, each a NASA visualization: ocean currents, night lights from 2012 to 2023, lightning seen from the Space Station, and a year of carbon dioxide. Press Listen and the page plays calm music made from what is on screen at that moment.

How it works: Each video frame is drawn to a hidden canvas and split into a 16 by 16 grid. For every cell the code measures colour, brightness, motion and track-specific signals: sea surface temperature from the colour scale, city light, yellow lightning flashes, orange carbon dioxide. Labels and colour bars are masked out. A scan line sweeps the map, and each value becomes a note in one calm musical key, panned left or right by its place on the map. Night lights, lightning and CO2 use fixed reference scales, so real change over time is audible instead of being normalised away.

Benefits and impact: Museums, classrooms and blind or low-vision listeners can experience NASA Earth data without needing to see it. Each track first explains what every sound means. Describe this moment gives a summary in words, Explore by touch plays and reads any place on the map, and Read aloud speaks everything. It works with keyboard and screen readers.

Creativity: The scan line works like a record needle playing the planet. A live dot drawing of Earth lights up wherever each note comes from, so sighted and blind visitors share the same moment.

Factors we considered: honesty to the data (no invented sound, fixed scales), accessibility first, calm sound that is pleasant for long listening, and mobile support.

Tools: HTML, CSS and JavaScript, Tone.js for sound, Canvas for frame analysis, GitHub Pages for hosting.
